title: Wadsworth v. Walmart — sanctions where the hallucinated citations came from a law firm's internal AI platform
author: Kelly H. Rankin

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Filing duties: AI use never displaces inquiry
st.an: Wadsworth accepts that AI-assisted filings remain governed by existing reasonable-inquiry and human-verification duties, and materially develops that proposition by treating the signing attorney’s responsibility as personal and nondelegable, extending it to authorised signatures, and showing how independent-verification safeguards can justify declining further firm-level sanctions.
qs: The key takeaway for attorneys is simple: make a reasonable inquiry into the law  before signing (or giving another permission to sign) a document, as required by Rule 11.

Since the Order to Show Cause, Morgan & Morgan has since  implemented an additional acknowledgement prior to using its AI software that “[u]sers  must independently verify” any AI-generated information before using or relying on it.

st.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
st.an: Wadsworth directly supports the cluster’s central distinction between valid-looking citations and reliable legal analysis. It treats AI as potentially useful while holding that lawyers’ existing duty of reasonable inquiry remains unchanged and requires reading authorities to confirm that they actually support the asserted propositions.
qs: The researcher must still read the case to  ensure the excerpt is existing law to support their propositions and arguments.
As attorneys transition to the world of AI, the duty to check their sources  and make a reasonable inquiry into existing law remains unchanged.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The court directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition that AI does not displace lawyers’ existing responsibility to verify authorities. Its treatment of eight nonexistent cases as a failure of reasonable inquiry—while separately finding counsel honest and forthcoming—also supports the view that sanctions analysis turns on verification and surrounding conduct rather than AI use alone.
qs: As attorneys transition to the world of AI, the duty to check their sources  and make a reasonable inquiry into existing law remains unchanged.
Nevertheless, the Court finds that Plaintiffs’ attorneys have been honest and forthcoming throughout this situation, and there is no reason to question what AI platform they claim was used.

st.t: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
st.an: The court accepts AI’s potential efficiency benefits but treats fabricated citations as a continuing reliability risk and source verification as an indispensable professional responsibility. Its efficiency statements are predictive rather than empirical, so it supports—without materially extending—the cluster’s core proposition that mitigation and useful assistance do not eliminate verification.
qs: 2 The instant case is simply the latest reminder to not blindly  rely on AI platforms’ citations regardless of profession.
While technology continues to evolve, one thing remains the same––checking and  verifying the source.

st.an: The decision strongly supports the cluster’s human-led, selective-deployment proposition. kp.k: AI's anticipated efficiencies remain conditional on responsible use
kp.d: Judge Kelly H. Rankin anticipates that AI could accelerate research and motion drafting, reduce client costs, and help courts analyze briefs and resolve cases more efficiently. These are prospective benefits, not measured findings; the order contrasts them with the present risk of fabricated sources.
qs: When done right, AI can be incredibly beneficial for attorneys and the public.
Courts will be able to efficiently analyze briefs and make correct rulings, which may speed up the judicial process for litigants.

kp.k: Internal AI generated eight nonexistent cases in one filing
kp.d: The January 22, 2025 motions in limine cited nine cases, eight of which did not exist. Ayala reportedly uploaded his draft to MX2.law, described cautiously by the court as an in-house Morgan & Morgan database, and requested additional supporting case law. He admitted using AI this way for the first time and incorporating the cases without verification. The court accepted the attorneys' account of the platform used and clarified that they apparently did not use ChatGPT. This is evidence of a specific sanctions incident, not a measured platform error rate.
qs: filed Motions in Limine that cited nine cases, but eight did not exist.
This website appears to be an in-house database launched by Mr. Ayala and Mr. Morgan’s firm, Morgan & Morgan.
Without verifying their accuracy, Mr. Ayala included the fake cases in the Motions in Limine.
It appears Plaintiffs’ attorneys did not use ChatGPT.

kp.k: AI leaves lawyers' source-verification obligations unchanged
kp.d: The court presents AI verification as a continuation of established legal research duties rather than a new obligation. Just as lawyers must read database results to distinguish operative law from arguments, dicta, or overruled authority, they must check AI-generated sources and reasonably investigate the law before relying on it.
qs: The researcher must still read the case to ensure the excerpt is existing law to support their propositions and arguments.
As attorneys transition to the world of AI, the duty to check their sources and make a reasonable inquiry into existing law remains unchanged.

kp.k: Fabricated authorities trigger Rule 11 without subjective bad faith
kp.d: Applying an objective-reasonableness standard, the court held that all three signing attorneys violated Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11(b)(2). Citing Mata, it reasoned that fictitious opinions cannot constitute existing law or a nonfrivolous basis for changing it. The order expressly states that subjective bad faith is unnecessary for sanctions.
qs: To find a Rule 11 violation, an attorney’s conduct is evaluated based on “objective reasonableness.”
Because there is no dispute that Respondents cited fake cases in a signed motion, Respondents’ conduct violates Rule 11(b)(2).
A finding of subjective bad faith is not required to impose sanctions.

kp.k: Signing lawyers cannot delegate reasonable inquiry to colleagues
kp.d: Morgan, the supervisor, and Goody, local counsel, did not draft or review the motions before filing, but their electronic signatures appeared on them. The court held that reliance on Ayala's experience did not discharge their nondelegable responsibilities. Its recommendation applies both to personally signing and authorizing another lawyer to sign: conduct reasonable inquiry or do not sign.
qs: Thus, blind reliance on another attorney can be an improper delegation of this duty and a violation of Rule 11.
Nevertheless, no inquiry cannot be deemed objectively reasonable even if the reliance is placed in an experienced attorney.
The key takeaway for attorneys is simple: make a reasonable inquiry into the law before signing (or giving another permission to sign) a document, as required by Rule 11.

kp.k: Citation anomalies offered opportunities to detect fabricated authorities
kp.d: The court identified absent pinpoint citations and missing full dates on unpublished authorities as warning signs that reviewing counsel could have noticed without knowing AI was used. It acknowledged that attorneys might not know every citation rule, while observing that copying citations by reference from Lexis or Westlaw supplies the full date.
qs: The hallucinated cases did not include any pinpoint citations.
Here, the hallucinated cases only contain the court and the year.
The hallucinations were certainly noticeable on the Motions’ face despite having no knowledge of the use of AI or Mr. Ayala’s reputation.

kp.k: Unverified AI output can damage clients and judicial resources
kp.d: The court found that withdrawal of the motions effectively deprived these clients of their opportunity to file meritorious motions in limine. Quoting Mata, it also emphasized broader harms from fabricated opinions: wasted opposing-party and court resources, reputational damage, and diminished confidence in the judicial system. Those broader harms are reasoning adopted from another decision, not separately quantified findings in this case.
qs: Respondents’ clients essentially lost their opportunity to file meritorious motions in limine, as they withdrew their Motions.
The opposing party wastes time and money in exposing the deception.
The Court’s time is taken from other important endeavors.
It promotes cynicism about the legal profession and the American judicial system.

kp.k: Sanctions differentiated drafting responsibility from supervisory and local roles
kp.d: The February 24, 2025 order revoked Ayala's pro hac vice admission, removed him as counsel of record, and fined him $3,000. Morgan and Goody each received $1,000 fines; Morgan retained his admission. The court weighed Ayala's proportion of fabricated citations, apparent research access, and existing professional awareness of AI hallucinations, while treating candor as mitigating. In revoking admission, it also considered that plaintiffs had at least five other attorneys and diminished risk of prejudice.
qs: As the drafter, Mr. Ayala will receive the highest sanction.
Mr. Ayala is removed as counsel of record.
A mitigating fact warranting a less severe punishment is Mr. Ayala’s honesty and candor.
Because Mr. Morgan was not the drafter, he will be sanctioned less severely.
The Court will also impose a sanction of a one-thousand-dollar ($1,000) fine on Ms. Goody.

kp.k: Candor and remediation mitigated but did not eliminate sanctions
kp.d: The court credited withdrawal of the motions, honesty about AI use, payment of opposing counsel's fees, and documented safeguards and training. It recommended these as minimum remedial steps in future incidents. Unlike the misleading responses described in Mata and Hayes, the respondents were forthcoming after the show-cause order, although the court noted they could have acted sooner after defendants flagged possible AI use on January 29, 2025.
qs: The Court appreciates Respondents’ remedial steps, transparency, and apologetic sentiments.
the Court recommends attorneys should––at the very least––follow these steps to remediate the situation prior to the issuance of any sanction.
The Court notes that Plaintiffs could have acted more swiftly.

kp.k: Firm training and verification safeguards limited additional disciplinary action
kp.d: Although Rule 11 provides for joint firm responsibility absent exceptional circumstances, the court declined to order either firm to show cause. Morgan & Morgan supplied evidence of prior training against Ayala's use of the software and added an acknowledgment requiring independent verification of AI-generated information. The court considered further sanctions greater than necessary. It likewise declined further action against Goody's firm, noting her lack of involvement in drafting and her statement that she did not use AI in practice.
qs: Here, Mr. Morgan submitted evidence showing that Morgan & Morgan trained its employees to not use the AI software in the way Mr. Ayala used it.
“[u]sers must independently verify”
The Court would have likely imposed sanctions similar to these measures. Thus, any further sanction would be greater than necessary.
Therefore, the law firms will not be ordered to show cause at this time.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Judge Kelly H. Rankin predicts conditional efficiency benefits from AI while holding that AI-assisted work does not change lawyers’ responsibility to verify legal authority.
pts.d: Rankin anticipates that properly used AI will help attorneys research and draft motions more quickly, potentially reducing client costs, and help courts analyze briefs and issue correct rulings more efficiently. These are predictions, not measured benefits. His present-tense findings concern the risks of unverified AI citations: in this case, a motion containing eight nonexistent cases out of nine cited cases led to sanctions against its drafter and two other signatories. The citations came from MX2.law, apparently Morgan & Morgan’s internal platform, rather than from direct use of ChatGPT. The court treats reasonable inquiry into legal authority as an unchanged, nondelegable obligation, including for signatories who did not draft the document or use AI themselves.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The risk and accountability claims rest on the case record and legal authority; the efficiency predictions have no quantitative evidence offered.
pts.d: The order relies on the filed motions, attorney responses, admissions that the cited cases were hallucinated, and evidence of the prompts and absence of verification. Ayala uploaded his draft to MX2.law and requested additional case law. The court also relies on Rule 11 and precedents concerning reasonable inquiry and sanctions, including Mata, Hayes and Gauthier; it expressly notes that Hayes was a criminal case and did not impose sanctions under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11. A Google Cloud explanation and a scientific-writing article supply background on hallucinations, not legal-tool performance measurements. Eight nonexistent citations among nine in this particular filing is case-specific evidence, not a benchmark or general hallucination rate. No data establish the predicted cost savings or judicial efficiency improvements.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The benefits are undated, conditional forecasts; the verification requirement and sanctions apply immediately in the February 24, 2025 order.
pts.d: The court describes lawyers as beginning to move into AI-assisted research and qualifies the potential benefits with 'When done right,' 'likely' and 'may,' without specifying an adoption or performance horizon. The underlying motion was filed January 22, 2025; the court issued its show-cause order February 6; respondents withdrew the motion the next day and admitted hallucinations February 10. Sanctions turn on failure to make a reasonable inquiry, not simply on AI use or subjective bad faith. Candor, withdrawal, payment of opposing counsel’s fees and preventive measures mitigated the response but did not eliminate individual sanctions. The court declined further proceedings against the firms, citing Morgan & Morgan’s existing training and new verification acknowledgment, and the circumstances of Goody’s noninvolvement.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: AI’s potential benefits extend to lawyers, clients and courts, while failures of verification expose drafters, supervising signatories and local counsel to sanctions and can impair clients’ litigation opportunities.
pts.d: Attorneys may gain research and drafting speed, clients may save costs, and litigants may experience faster judicial processes. In this case, Ayala was removed as counsel through revocation of his pro hac vice admission and fined $3,000. Morgan and local counsel Goody were each fined $1,000 despite not drafting or reviewing the motion; their responsibility arose from signing without reasonable inquiry. The court states that withdrawal effectively cost the clients their opportunity to file meritorious motions in limine. Opposing counsel incurred fees that respondents paid. Morgan & Morgan implemented additional safeguards for its internal AI software. The order illustrates that neither an internal platform nor reliance on an experienced colleague removes the human signatory’s responsibility.
